newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain's Hanley objects to repealing HK laws.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Hanley objects to repealing HK laws.

text.p: Britain on Wednesday reiterated its opposition to China's plan to roll back civil liberties in Hong Kong after the British colony returns to Chinese rule this year.

Earlier this month, the China-appointed body in charge of the handover proposed scrapping or amending 25 laws and articles when Beijing resumes control of the territory. Some of the laws include parts of the Bill of Rights and laws allowing freedom of assembly and association.
The body said changes were warranted because the laws contravened the Basic Law, the territory's post-colonial mini-constitution promulgated by Beijing in 1990.

"We see, and indeed I think no serious lawyer disagrees, that the Bill of Rights ordinance is consistent to the Basic Law and that the Basic Law takes supremacy," Jeremy Hanley, Britain's minister of state at the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, told reporters on his arrival in Hong Kong for a three-day visit.
"And therefore the reasons given for the proposed actions, we think are totally inconsistent with the legislation which we all agree," said the British minister responsible for Hong Kong.

"We will certainly be discussing it at every level and the (British) Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind will be discussing it I hope very shortly with the (Chinese) Vice Premier (and Foreign Minister) Qian Qichen," Hanley said.
The British Foreign Secretary will visit the territory between February 15 and 18, Hanley was quoted as saying.
Rifkind will meet Qian in Singapore in the middle of next month to discuss the proposals to dilute Hong Kong laws and the provisional legislature, local media quoted Hanley as saying.
Last week, Hanley summoned the London-based Chinese ambassador Jiang Enzhu to express Britain's concern over the proposals to dilute laws guaranteeing civil liberties in the territory.
Hanley said Britain enjoyed an "excellent" relationship with China despite the clashes over the proposals.
"We are, I think, friendly enough to be honest with each other....Now here we are being honest enough to say to them, we think you are mistaken," Hanley said.
Hanley also reiterated Britain's opposition to a provisional legislature picked by a Chinese-appointed panel in December.
The provisional legsialture will replace the current elected chamber when Britain hands the colony back to China on July 1, after more than 150 years of British rule.
Britain has refused to recognise the interim body, saying it has no basis in the handover treaty or in the Basic Law that was agreed between London and Beijing.
